transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

I guess… what finally pushed me to come in is that I don’t feel like myself in this very quiet way. Like the part of me that used to reach for people, or get something back from my work, has sort of gone dim.

I’m still doing what I’m supposed to do, mostly. I go through obligations. But yoga, galleries, journaling—things that used to feel like they filled me up—now I just don’t really… feel much from them. It’s strange, because I used to tell clients all the time about small routines and connection and meaning, and now I’ll buy a new notebook and it just sits there. Actually, I have this whole drawer of notebooks, which is ridiculous, but anyway… that’s the main thing. I feel like I’m moving through things rather than living in them.
How long have you been feeling this way—weeks, months, or longer?

I’d say… months. About eight months, I think. It started around when we took my older relative into our apartment, and since then the whole way I’m thinking and working and being with people just feels different. I keep trying to pinpoint a day, but it wasn’t really like that—it was more like the apartment changed, the routines changed, and then I looked up and realized I’d changed too.
Aside from the loss of interest and pleasure, have you also been feeling sad, empty, or down for most of the day, nearly every day, during these past eight months?

I don’t know if I’d call it sad, exactly. Empty maybe… but even that word feels a little too neat. It’s more like I’m muted.

Most of the day, nearly every day—when you say it like that, I start trying to calculate it, which is probably not helpful. I’ll have moments where I’m fine, like if I’m making tea or noticing some weird little thing outside the window, and then I think, “See, I’m okay.” But then the rest of the day feels kind of flat.

Sorry, I’m not answering cleanly. I guess I haven’t been crying all the time or anything. It’s more just… not much seems to land.
Besides feeling muted or flat, have you noticed changes in your energy, concentration, sleep, or appetite over these past eight months?

Um… I’m not sure I can separate those out very well. Like, energy versus motivation versus just being tired of the same rooms, you know?

Sleep—well, I notice it more when my neighbor’s hallway light flickers under the door, which is such a small thing, but once I see it I can’t unsee it. And then I start thinking about whether we should change the curtains, or whether the plant near the window is dying because I moved it. Sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I guess I haven’t been tracking appetite or anything. Concentration… sometimes I feel like I’m reading the same paragraph twice, but I don’t know if that’s new or just me being distracted. So, I don’t have a clear answer. Nothing where I thought, “Oh, this is a big change,” exactly.
Have you been having thoughts that you're worthless, or feeling excessively guilty about things, or feeling hopeless about the future during these past eight months?

Worthless… I don’t know. That’s a heavy word. I wouldn’t say I walk around thinking that exactly.

Guilty, maybe in the normal way? Like if I forget to call someone back, or I snap because the kitchen is too crowded, then I’ll replay it longer than I probably need to. But I don’t know if that’s “excessive” or just… being a person in a small apartment with everyone’s habits rubbing up against each other.

Hopeless about the future… I don’t really think that far ahead lately. Not in a dramatic way. It’s more like the future is sort of foggy, like when you’re trying to plan dinner but you first have to move three things off the counter, and then you notice the mail pile, and suddenly it’s not about dinner anymore. So… I’m not sure I’d call it hopeless. I haven’t really noticed thoughts like that clearly.

Over these past eight months, has this 'muted' feeling actually interfered with your ability to do your job, care for your family, or manage daily responsibilities, or have you still been able to keep up with everything as usual?

I’m still showing up, mostly. Like, I haven’t disappeared or stopped doing the basic things. I get dressed, I go to work, I answer emails… eventually.

But it’s not exactly “as usual.” There have been a couple grant deadlines I missed, which is embarrassing because that used to be the kind of thing I could keep in my head, or at least on three different sticky notes. And my supervisor hasn’t said it outright in a harsh way, but she’s… shifted some of my more complicated clients to other clinicians. Quietly. Like she’s trying not to make it a thing.

So I guess I’m functioning, but not at my normal level. It’s hard to say that without wanting to explain it away.

Have you noticed any difference in how you feel on days or times when you're away from the apartment and the caregiving situation—for example, during a weekend trip or a day fully at work—versus when you're at home dealing with it?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed a clean difference like that. I mean, work has its own noise, you know? The printer, people knocking, the little crisis pile that builds up before lunch… so I can’t say I feel suddenly lighter just because I’m not at the apartment.

And I haven’t really had, like, a real weekend trip where I could compare it. I keep thinking we should go somewhere, even just a cheap motel with bad coffee, but then there’s the question of who covers what, and whether the cat feeder still works—sorry.

So… I don’t know. Maybe I’m a little less caught in it when I’m fully occupied somewhere else, but I haven’t tracked it enough to say. At home I’m more aware of everything that needs doing, but that might just be because I’m there looking at it.
Focusing just on sleep: compared to eight months ago, are you now taking longer to fall asleep, waking up in the middle of the night, or waking up much earlier than you want to, on most nights?

Sleep… I’m not sure I have a clean answer for that. I mean, I go to bed, and sometimes I’m thinking about whether I set the coffee up or if the laundry is still in the washer, and then I’ll remember something totally unrelated, like this one client years ago who always wore purple scarves—sorry, that’s not what you asked.

Compared to eight months ago… I haven’t really been tracking it. I don’t think I’m waking up dramatically early every day or anything that obvious. Falling asleep maybe depends on the night? Some nights I’m out, some nights I lie there a while, but I couldn’t honestly say it’s most nights or that it’s a big change.

So… I guess I haven’t noticed a clear sleep pattern change.
Have you noticed any change in your appetite or your weight—either eating more or less than usual, or gaining or losing weight—over these past eight months?

I don’t think so? Not in a way I’ve really noticed. My appetite is… kind of ordinary, I guess. Some days I forget lunch because the day gets away from me, but that happened before too, especially if I’m doing paperwork and then suddenly it’s 3:40 and the yogurt I brought is still sitting there.

Weight-wise, I don’t weigh myself regularly. We have a scale but it’s under a stack of towels in the bathroom because the closet shelf broke—well, not broke, exactly, it’s just sagging. Anyway, my clothes fit about the same, so I don’t think there’s been a big gain or loss. Nothing obvious.
Regardless of motivation, have you been feeling physically tired or low in energy nearly every day over these past eight months—for example, feeling drained even after resting?

I don’t know that I’d call it nearly every day. I mean, I get tired, sure, but everyone says that, don’t they? Especially by the end of the day when there’s still dishes and the mail pile and that one envelope you keep moving from table to table instead of opening.

But drained even after resting… I’m not sure. Sometimes I rest and then I just feel sort of annoyed that I used up the time resting, which is different from being physically exhausted, I think. I haven’t noticed a clear, constant low-energy thing over the whole eight months. Nothing I could point to and say, “Yes, that’s happening almost every day.”

{"intent": "Assess for psychomotor changes (a core depressive symptom not yet explored) to determine if enough symptoms are present to meet full criteria for a major depressive episode versus a subthreshold presentation more consistent with adjustment disorder.", "question": "Have others—or you yourself—noticed you moving or speaking more slow

Slower… like physically slowed down? I don’t think anyone’s said that to me. I mean, people at work will sometimes say I seem distracted, but that’s not the same thing, and honestly everyone seems distracted lately—half our staff meetings are just people looking for the Teams link that was already in the email.

Speaking more slowly… I haven’t noticed that. I can ramble, obviously, but that’s not new. And moving slowly, no, not in a way I’d point to. I don’t think there’s been some obvious change where I’m dragging around or people are commenting on it.
Does the way you've been feeling seem out of proportion to the caregiving stress itself, or does it feel like a reasonable reaction to everything that's changed since your relative moved in?

I’m not sure how to measure “out of proportion,” honestly. Some days I think, well, of course I’m upset—having someone move in changes the whole rhythm of the house, like where the mugs go and whether the TV is on during dinner, which sounds tiny but it’s not tiny when it’s every day.

But then I second-guess it, because maybe I should be handling it better. I work with people dealing with big life stuff all the time, so I get into this weird comparison thing, like, “This isn’t that bad,” and then I’m annoyed at myself for even thinking that. So… I don’t know. It feels related to the caregiving, definitely. Whether it’s more than a reasonable reaction, I can’t really say.
Over these past eight months, have you had any thoughts of death, of not wanting to be alive, or of harming yourself?

No… I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had moments where I feel overwhelmed and think, “I need everything to stop for five minutes,” but not in the sense of wanting to be dead or hurting myself.

It’s more like wanting quiet, or wanting nobody to ask me where the good towels are, which is… not the same thing. So, no, I haven’t had thoughts of harming myself or not wanting to be alive.

I don’t really know how to answer beyond… I don’t think that’s where my mind has been going. When I get overwhelmed, it’s more like I want the noise and the demands to pause, like when three people are talking at once and the dishwasher is beeping and someone can’t find the insurance card—those ridiculous little pileups.

But I haven’t been sitting there making plans or thinking in that direction, if that’s what you mean. It’s more exhaustion than anything dramatic.

I’m not sure what you’re asking me there—if you mean whether there’s more to it than being tired and irritated, I don’t know. It’s hard to separate out, because everything kind of blends together after a while.

Like, I’ll start thinking I’m upset about one thing, and then suddenly I’m remembering that the hallway closet still has boxes in it from when they moved in, and then I’m mad about the boxes instead of the original thing. So… I may need you to ask it a little more directly.
